title: Ratings Versus Rankings
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The article contrasts ratings, which measure people against a standard, with rankings, which compare colleagues to one another. Leaders are tempted to rank to celebrate top performers and apply peer pressure, but the author argues rankings breed jealousy, damage team goodwill and demotivate everyone who is not on top. Because only a few can win, rankings showcase losers more than winners. The recommended alternative is a criterion system in which success means reaching a defined level regardless of others' results. The author cites research that people in rating systems share the processes behind their success more readily. The closing call is to drop the urge to rank and to rate performance so everyone can reach the highest standards.
points: Rankings pit colleagues against each other and erode the climate that sustains long-term team performance.
Because few can place highly, rankings leave the majority seeing themselves as perpetual underperformers.
A criterion system lets any number of people succeed independent of what others accomplish.
Research is cited to show that team members under ratings are more likely to share the practices behind their success.
quotes: To celebrate top performers and to apply peer pressure on the rest of the team, leaders are sometimes tempted to rank team members in the performance evaluation process. Whereas ratings allow team members to judge themselves against a standard, rankings force colleagues to compare themselves to others, rather than to absolute results.

This pits team members against one another and often produces competitive jealousy, bitterness, and bad feelings between colleagues. Rankings too often undermine the goodwill and spirit of the team and result in a negative climate that actually decreases the long-term performance of the majority of the team.

Since there can only be one top performer and only a limited number of high-ranking winners, rankings demotivate those who begin to see themselves as perpetual underperformers. Rankings showcase losers more than they highlight winners.

The goal of great teams is to have all A players and winners. This is where ratings against a set of standards come to the rescue. The motivating alternative to a ranking system is a criterion system where success is determined by whether people reach a specific level, target, or goal independent of what others accomplish.

Not only do ratings motivate people to perform at a higher level, but research has also shown that team members in a rating system are more likely to share with their colleagues the processes and actions that led to their success. With an unlimited number of winners, team members come to know exactly what is required of them to earn the recognition and reward they deserve through performance.
It’s time to dump the urge to rank people and commit to the advantages of rating performance. Ratings are the points of a compass that show everyone the path to higher performance.
